A student concludes that the answer to 99 + 1 is 910 because of the failure to 'carry' the 1.

Students report using mental representations of 'finger like' objects to invoke double counting procedures for arithmetic combinations, whereas high achievers see numerical symbols 'flashing' to flexibly recall derived facts.
For combinations like 7 + 6, where the first addend is larger, students used the rote rule 'Double the first addend and add 1'.
To estimate '15 is what percent of 33', a preservice teacher applies the wrong concept by calculating .15 x 30.
When calculating the number of kittens, a student might write '2.4 kittens', or for the number of buses needed, a student might write 'Nine-point-two-two-five buses'.

When evaluating a peer's decimal answer of '19.21429 trips' for a lift, many children accepted it as correct because 'the calculator says that' or because it was the exact arithmetic division of 269 by 14.
After time at the site two students 'moved the decimals' and then, in the end, moved them back, getting 0.08 as their (incorrect) answer [for 0.4 divided by 0.05].

Given 741 x 12 = 8892, to find 74.1 x 12, the student writes 88.92 because 'in seventy-four point one there was two numbers before the decimal point so I made the two numbers before the decimal point in my answer'.

A student splits 60 (represented by six ten-blocks) into two groups of three tens. When prompted to fix it, he moves blocks to create three unequal groups (one group of ten, one of twenty, one of thirty) and justifies it by saying 'Cause then, this would belong over here...'

A sixth grader attempting to share 28 marbles among 4 boys tried the division algorithm, rejected the answer 0.14, tried a multiplication algorithm resulting in 112, and ultimately rejected the known fact '7x4=28' because she could not understand how it applied to the situation.

A third grader solving '28 marbles, 7 boys' grouped the marbles as 'seven and seven... twenty-eight', arriving at 4, but when asked why he chose seven, he incorrectly explained he was giving 7 marbles to one boy, realizing there were not enough marbles for all boys.
When dividing 8645834 by 2, a student divides 5 by 2 to yield '2.5' in the middle of the quotient, and similarly divides 3 by 2 to yield '1.5', failing to abide by the place notation system.

A student correctly identifies the pattern for '0 3 6 9 12' as 'goes up by three', but when solving problems individually, they rely on adding and do not relate the skip counting to multiplication facts.
"In the two sets above you can see that 7 pieces is greater than 6 pieces, so 7/8 is larger than 6/7."
A Year 5 child in the MAB group was confused to such an extent that he named minis 'ones' and the large blocks 'thousandths.'
A hypothetical student claims 7/8 is larger than 3/8 simply because 'one is seven and one is three,' failing to acknowledge the 'eighth-sized' fractional unit.
A student asks 'Ma'am, oneths kyun nahi hota? [Teacher, why are there no oneths?]' and another justifies that oneths would be 'one by one'.

A student asks 'Why don't they say the thing instead of a fraction?' and later states, 'I still don't get what 3/12 is... if you take it from the market and you buy it, and you have 3 of them, that's 3 oranges.'

A student calculated 7.31 - 6.4 as 1.27, or attempted to calculate it as 'four minus one... three minus six', struggling because the digits didn't form matching whole-number pairs on both sides of the decimal.
A student claimed 7.89 is bigger than 7.9 because 'eight nine is bigger than nine.'
A student did not understand what a peer meant by "half of the price" when trying to compute the price of the garage for different sets.
A student explained their addition method by saying, 'I just thought about it as doing it without the decimal and then I just added the decimal at the end.'
A student ordered the integer cards correctly (e.g., -8, -4, -2, 1, 5, 7) but then said that 'eight' was the greatest and 'one' was the least.
A student reasoned, 'The difference between 2 and 3 is 1. Then the fraction after 2/5 is 3/5. Therefore, there is no fraction between 2/5 and 3/5.'
A student responded that 'In 0.435: 4 represents 400, 3 represents 30 and 5 represents 5' based on the assumption that 4 is hundredths, 3 is tenths, and 5 is oneths.
A student selected .42 as larger than .5 and explained that 'forty-two is bigger than five.'

A student stated 'the bigger the numerator . . . the bigger the denominator' when trying to explain why 5/7 is bigger than 1/7, reflecting the theorem-in-action 'The bigger the denominator the bigger the fraction'.
A student states 'One fifth is less ... because five is less than nine.'
A student wrote .8 as the answer to 5 + .3 and explained that 'five plus three is eight, and the point stays right in front of it.'

A student wrote the number sentence '2/4 + 1/4 = 3' and explained that the '3' stood for 'three fourths of a pizza,' insisting that 'five eighths as five or I can write it as five eighths. It doesn't matter.'
Afwandi explains that .008000 is the greatest value because 'The zeros in front don't mean anything, but it has zero's in the back and that means that it is (8,000)-eight thousand'.
An average speed of 11.9 miles per hour was read as '11 miles 9 minutes per hour'; and 'pork chops weighting 1.07 lb' was read as '1 lb 7 ounces'.
Answering 'two-ninths' to the problem of finding the sum of one-third and one-sixth, by adding numerators (1+1=2) and denominators (3+6=9).
Anthony asserts that '.8 is 1/8 of a whole', incorrectly converting the decimal by changing the decimal point to a fraction bar.
Asserting that 0.021 is higher than 0.87 because 'it has more digits behind the decimal point'.
Asserting that 0.1815 is the greatest value among 0.09, 0.365, 0.4 and 0.1815 because they are using the rule 'more digits makes bigger'.
Believing 7 is larger than 7.1 because 7.1 means '7 whole ones and you knock off point 1'.
Believing a person who measured a window as 'six hand-spans' has a bigger hand than one who measured it as 'five hand-spans' because six is a bigger number than five.
Calculating 1/10 of 20 as 10 because 'Twenty is in the tens table', and 1/2 of 50 as 5.
Children adding fractions tend to 'add tops and bottoms' separately, or judge that 4/8 is larger than 2/4 by focusing on the magnitudes of the individual numbers rather than the ratio they form.
Claiming that 4.63 is bigger than 4.8 'because 63 is bigger than 8'.
Claire explained regrouping in 527 - 135 by stating 'You change the 5 to the number below it, which is 4. And you mark a 1, which makes this 12', failing to relate the digits to hundreds or tens.
Converting fractions to percentages to order them and consciously rounding one eighth to thirteen percent because percentages 'seem like whole numbers'.
For a moment, Michael interpreted 'two tenths' as 'two 10s' and got his answer of 20 cents.
For the CD task stating 'Sam's stack is 2/5 of that height [Theo's stack]', students operating at Stage 2 wrote 'S + 3/5 = T' instead of 'S = 2/5T'.
For the pair 3/4 and 7/9, a student chooses 3/4 because it has a 'smaller gap' or claims 5/6 and 7/8 are the 'same because each has one left'.
For the problem 'I spent 900 lire for 0.75 hg of cocoa. What is the price of 1 hg?', students frequently incorrectly chose 900 x 0.75 instead of 900 ÷ 0.75.
For the problem 1 - 4/5, a student read it as 'one minus four fifths' but interpreted the '1' as 'one fifth' and got an answer of three fifths by calculating 'four... take one away'.
If it was equal to it would be one whole unit... if it was a whole they'd call it a whole, they call it one.
In response to the problem 6 + c = 4, a student said, 'What's that plus for? Isn't it supposed to be a minus?'
Johnny claimed 'zero is not divisible by anything so it can't be even' and stated during the interview that 'you don't really have anything to divide from.'
Kimberley argued that a complex incorrect inequality sequence could still be deduced simply because she "could switch the middle two terms" and it "feels intuitive to us, but it is not right."
Kwok Chung replied that '0.384 was bigger than 0.32 because 384 in 0.384 was three hundred and eighty-four, which is bigger than thirty-two in 0.32'.
Lucas wrote 7/2 to mean 'seven and a half', explaining 'I know to put a 2 cause one and a half has a 2.'
Naming the red rod 'one-half' of the orange rod because the student knew the white rod was half of the red rod, erroneously applying that half relationship to the orange rod context.
Naming the white rod 'ten' instead of 'one-tenth' because the orange rod is equivalent to ten white rods.

Nathan calculated 2/3 times 4/5 as 8/15 using the standard algorithm but could not connect this to his operational scheme, instead pulling out two separate fraction bars and stating he would put an 'x' between them.

Objecting to a peer constructing a 1/16 fraction out of a single square on a geoboard (and subsequently 1/32 from a half-square), arguing 'he ain't using the whole square' and 'There's not thirty-two squares.'
One third is less than one fourth "because three is less than four."
Ordering fractions by finding the 'lowest numbers' when numerators are the same, or stating 4/35 is smaller than 4/29 because 'nothing times 29 equals 35 and it has lower numbers'.
Rachel chose 2/5 to be larger than 1/2 because 'for a start off the top number's larger, and the bottom is as well.'
Responding '3.2' instead of '3.4' when identifying a decimal on a number line where the subunit was five, or answering '2.3' instead of '2.03' when the calibration is between 2.0 and 2.1.
Sheena argues zero could be even because the numbers on each side (1 and -1) are odd. Sean argues zero is not even because 'what two things can you put together to make it?'
Siu Wai responded that 'in 0.354, 3 is tens and represents 30, 5 is hundreds and represents 500, 4 is thousands and represents 4000'.
Stating 'When indeed do you divide by 2/3?' because the teacher could only envision division as dividing a quantity into a whole number of parts.
Stating that 0.34 is larger than 0.8 because 'thirty-four has two numbers and point eight has only one.'

Stating that the product of 3, 17, and 19 cannot be a perfect square because odd numbers 'can't be whole numbers when they're square rooted', whereas the product of 2, 12, and 16 has a 'good chance' of being a perfect square because they are even.
Student 4 explained that one-third is bigger than one-half because 'Three is higher than two.'
Students claimed 2y was larger than y because '2y is greater because it is two times more than y' and '2y because it has a number in front of the letter.'
Students held the theorem-in-action: 'The biggest fraction is the one that has the biggest number of parts'.
Students struggle to choose the correct operation for '1 kilo of detergent makes 15 kilos of soap. How much soap can be made from 0.75 kilos of detergent?' because 0.75 acts as the operator.
Subtracting 0.552 from 0.938 by doing 938 - 552 = 386 and blindly copying the 'period and zero' because they appeared in the original numbers.
Suggesting 'two fifths and three fifths' and 'one third and two thirds' as pairs of numbers that add up to five.
Taylor crossed out the numeral seven to show 'seven and a half', visually representing a seven cut in half rather than seven whole units plus an additional half unit.
The student initially named a 6-stick as 'one-sixth' of a 24-stick, rather than one-fourth.
The teacher writes two fractions on the board, '1/7' and '1/5,' and asks which one is larger. To the teacher's surprise, most of the students claim that 1/7 is larger because 7 is larger than 5.
Three fifths is less than six tenths because "3 is less than 6, and 5 is less than 10."
Three students knew that 0.05 is larger than 0.025, but considered that dividing by a decimal 'reverses the rule of division.' That is, 'dividing by a larger decimal makes the quotient larger.'

To find 1/4 of 1/2 of a cookie, a student splits the half into 4 parts, and reasons 'if this [one half] is four [pieces], this whole thing is eight [pieces], and I gave her one part out of eight,' treating the pieces as counting units.
To find a 40% discount on 89€, the student Francisco writes '89 - 40% = 49€', treating the percentage as an absolute currency value.
To solve the equation 8t - 9 = t + 12, a student says 'Take nine off both sides' and incorrectly replaces the 12 with a 3, leading to the erroneous equation 7t = 3.
When a 3-stick was iterated 8 times to make a 24-stick, the children called the 3-stick 'three-eighths' of the 24-stick instead of 'one-eighth'.
When a beam was 13 A-units and the B-unit was 4 A-units, Barry stated 'Four times nothing equals thirteen!' and 'His B unit's too long', treating the remainder as an unmeasurable leftover.
When adjusting an apple cake recipe for 10 people, a student calculates 6.666 eggs and refuses to round to 7 eggs, arguing that 'This comes from a recipe book! It must be exact.'
When asked 'What is five fourteenths of 322?', Kylie responded 'Nope' when asked if she had any idea how to do it, despite successfully doing similar calculations in prior sessions.
When asked if 7 is 3/4 of 10, a student replied, 'Yes, 7 is 3/4 of 10 because 3 plus 4 equals 7.'

When asked the meaning of the symbolic representation 1/3, a student explained it meant 'three pieces or one pizza that's cut into three pieces,' or interpreted 3/5 as 'three whole pumpkin pies with five pieces in each pie.'

When asked to apply a 1/2 multiplier to a 1/3 bar using the MULTIPLY button, Kylie stated, 'it wouldn't be exactly timesing, it would be more like dividing... you can't really... make, um... a third by multiplying.'
When asked to circle 1/3 of 12 strawberries, a pupil circled exactly three strawberries. Similarly, when asked for 2/3 of 12, a pupil answered 'six' (two groups of three).
When asked to collect 2/3 of 12 swap cards, Simpson took 6 cards, stating 'I have two groups and there's three in the group.'
When asked to compare 1/6 and 1/8, a student answered 'One eighth is bigger' and explained, '[Eight] is a bigger number I think. [Eight] is bigger than [six].'
When asked to compare 2/3 and 3/4, a student reasoned, 'They are both the same size because they both have one piece missing.' Another claimed there is no number between decimal 3 and decimal 4.

When asked to compare 8/24 with 13/39 in her first interview, Angela reasoned, 'The 39 is larger, and so it's gonna make the pieces really small.' She concluded that 8/24 was greater without explicitly accounting for the numerators in any way.
When asked to define an irrational number, twenty-eight percent of 9th graders gave answers like '..which is not a whole number'.
When asked to draw 7/5 of a candy bar, Bridget marked the bar into five parts, added two more pieces, and said 'they turned into seven pieces instead of five pieces'.

When asked to estimate the location of 11/12 - 4/6 on a number line, a student attempted to calculate an exact answer with a faulty algorithm: 'I took 11 - 4 = 7. I added 12 and 6 and got 18 so I got 7/18 and I thought 11/18 is between 1/2 and 1.'

When asked to evaluate 3/4 / 1/2 using a number line, a student argued 'you can't use two fractions on a number line,' while another stated 'It doesn't start with a whole number so you don't know how long to make the line.'
When asked to evaluate the statement '10 ÷ .65 is greater than 10' without computing, subjects incorrectly claimed the quotient must be less than 10 because 'division always makes smaller.'

When asked to make a 3/3-bar into a 9/8-bar, Bridget suggested making eight more 24-part bars 'so you'd have nine-eighths,' treating nine-eighths as a unit of nine units without forming eight of those units as equal to the unit bar.

When asked to make a bar 11/4 times as long as a 3-m bar, the student divided each 1-m part into four pieces, copied the 3-m bar three times, and removed a 1-m part, ending up with '11 of 4/4 of 1 m' instead of 11/4 of 3 m.
When asked to make a bar 6/5 of a unit long, Barry made 5/6 and asserted, 'That's impossible. You mean five sixths? The denominator, cannot be smaller than the... [numerator].'

When asked to place '1' on a number line that shows a longer interval, students might place '1' at the very end of the visible line, or they might determine a fraction's value by counting the number of tick marks instead of spaces.

When asked to pose a word problem for '8 2/3 ÷ 1/4 = ?', a teacher wrote an equal-group multiplication problem: 'Some apples were shared among 4 people. Each person got 8 2/3 bags. How many bags (of apples) are there in the beginning?', which actually represents 8 2/3 × 4.

When asked to solve 5 + .3, a student says 'Five and three is eight and there's one place for the decimal point so I put it right there' yielding .8. Or completing .58 = .5 + ___ with .53 because 'Five plus fifty-three would equal fifty-eight.'
When asked what '2.37 km' means, a student answers 'Two kilometers and thirty seven meters', incorrectly reading the decimal digits '.37' as a whole number of meters.
When asked what fraction two 1/7 pieces (4-sticks) would make together, the student answered 'One-fourteenth... because you add one-seventh and another seventh it makes 14.'
When asked what two-thirds means in the context of finding a fraction of six sweets, Rachel replied 'Twos into the number?', applying a whole-number division rule rather than partitioning.
When asked which is bigger between 1/3 and 1/4, a student answers '1/3 is bigger because 4 is more than 3'.

When asked which is larger, 4/15 or 4/10, a student responded '4/15' and reasoned 'Because 10 is less than 15.' Another student reasoned, 'If you take 4 from 15 it's 11; if you take 4 from 10 that's 6. 6 is way smaller than 11.'

When attempting to pose a problem for 2/3 * 1/2, stating 'there are 2 cakes' and 'cut the cake into thirds', which separates the fraction into parts rather than referring directly to the fraction as a quantity. Alternatively, creating a problem using only whole numbers to avoid the fractions entirely.
When comparing 1020.0 and 102.00, students initially state they might be the same 'because the number of zeroes are same [ignoring the decimal point].'
When comparing 3.3 and 3.300, a student (Soh) concludes that 3.3 is greater, reasoning that '3.300 is less than 3.3 because it has more numbers [digits]'.
When comparing 4/7 and 4/5, students choose 4/7 as larger because of 'larger numbers', demonstrating a form of whole number dominance.
When comparing 6/14 and 6/15, the student incorrectly states that 6/15 is larger 'Because 15 is greater than 14.'
When determining what fraction of two 12-slice pizzas is eaten by 7 students who each eat two slices, a student rejects the answer 14/24, incorrectly insisting 'You can't change the 12. It's 14/12.'

When explaining 527 - 135, Jamie stated, 'But I don't know why that [4 remaining in the hundred's place] would be 400, if you're only borrowing 10,' incorrectly interpreting the 10 in the tens place as 10 ones instead of 100 ones.
When finding the sum of 1/3 and 1/4, Jason initially said 'One seventh' then 'two sevenths', before rejecting them because they represented a smaller part than the individual components.

When given 'The following bar is 5/7 of another bar. Make the other bar.', Michael initially partitioned the given bar into 7 pieces instead of 5, failing to see that the 5 equal parts each represented a seventh of the new bar.
When given 24 oz ÷ 1/4 h, drawing 4 rows with 6 items each and concluding the answer is 6 oz per 1/4 hour, treating '24' as the amount for a full hour and '1/4' as an instruction to make 4 groups.
When given 5 + [ ] = 3, Violet stated: 'There's no way to do that. ... Because you have to do 5 minus something equals 2. If you add to that, say 5 plus 2, that would be 7 not 3.'
When given the problem '1 m of suit fabric costs 15 000 lire. How much does 0.75 m cost?', students frequently incorrectly chose 15 000 ÷ 0.75 or 15 000 + 0.75 instead of 15 000 x 0.75.
When given the problem '70 ÷ 1/2', a student argued the quotient is less than 70 because '70 is being divided into parts, the quotient (the answer) will be less than 70.'
When iterating a 1/8 piece nine times to produce a 9/8 stick, students named the result 'nine ninths' or 'a whole', shifting their reference whole to the newly created 9-part stick.
When judging 689 x 33 = 22,737, students claimed 'the answer is thousands' or 'this is a very large answer' to justify it being unreasonable.
When moving to decimal division, students "saw only the three [remainder]. They didn't see the three over four... because with remainder we write 3 in brackets."

When presented with the expression 3 / 4, a student says 'You can't do that... you can't turn divided by around,' and another argues that if 3 cakes are shared among 4 people, 'One person won't get any.'
When presented with the symbolic problem 1 - 4/5, Ted answered 'three-fifths', appearing to think of the '1' as one-fifth and subtracting it from four-fifths.
After the teacher explains adding (+4) and (-1) using right and left arrows on a number line, the student replies, 'So, no, this, I don't have problem with this. Just minus or plus?'
One student counted backward, 'Five, four, three, two, one'. He ordered the first set of integers by absolute value, and explained, 'Zero, one, two. Two, three, then four, five, six, seven, eight.'
When asked what minus twelve plus twelve is, a student responded, 'It's 24. You're supposed to add twelve.'
When asked how many 4s were in two 12s, Cody computed the total (24) and replied, 'It could be 6, or 8 three times, because 8 times 3 is 24 too.'
When making skipping ropes from string so that it was 'all used up and each doll gets an even share,' some children made two cuts, resulting in leftover material.

To calculate 16 · 25, Ida multiplied the tens (10 · 20) and then the units (6 · 5), adding them together and explaining that 'one doesn't need to calculate all at once, as long as it will be the same number'.
When asked if the order of moves matters, a student responded, 'yes...it's a bit like when I do two plus three equals five... and three plus two is also equal to five'.

Despite knowing that commutativity is valid, Ida exhibited wavering utilization of the property when evaluating calculations, tentatively stating 'it depends on which way one does it... or no, it doesn't matter which way one does it'.

A student pointed to locations on a number line where characters stopped to show their journey, but performed the long division calculations in a separate physical space without linking the 'groups of' partitioning process to the diagram.

When subtracting 1997 from 3002, students struggle with 'borrowing across zero' in the decomposition method or 'incrementing the 9-digit' in the equal addition method. Another example is 'borrowing from the tens column when it was unnecessary' (e.g., 37 - 4 = 23).
When calculating 32 - 23, a student explains that the difference is 11 because '3 take away 2 is 1, and 2 take away 3 is 1.'
When performing 256 - 17, a student used the 'smaller from larger' bug, taking 6 from 7 to get 1, and 1 from 5 to get 4, resulting in an answer of 241.

deduplication.rule: Normalized text is kept in the first arm in literature, student, authored order; repeated rows within one arm remain because they carry corpus bindings.

description: A fixed recognition benchmark built from labels already carried by the strategy corpus.
